description: What each fixture pins. A fixture under valid/ must be accepted by the schema named beside it. A fixture under invalid/ must be refused; refused_by says by what. schema means the JSON Schema document alone refuses it, and a consumer can assert that with a validator and nothing else. validator means the documentation states the rule but JSON Schema cannot express it, because it needs the graph, the brick manifest, the included file or the expression language; those fixtures are schema valid on purpose and are refused by the workflow validator instead.
notes: Read the fixtures with a YAML 1.2 parser. The trigger block is spelled on:, as the documentation spells it, and a YAML 1.1 parser reads that bare key as the boolean true. A loader that does so will fail every fixture carrying a trigger, and will do the same to the workflows people write.

Digests are written out in full. The documentation elides them in the middle, as 9f2c1d...b7e0, which is a typographic elision and not a value; the fixtures keep the first and last characters and fill the rest so that each one is a well formed sha256.
A fixture carrying a manifest key is checked against a brick manifest that lives elsewhere in this corpus. The rule it pins is about the two documents together, so neither file alone shows it.

An included file is a fragment and never an entry point, so the fragment group holds its fixtures to workflow.schema.json#/$defs/fragment rather than to the document's root, which is for the entry point and would refuse every one of them for lacking apiVersion. mcp-in-included-file.yaml is among them: the definition refuses mcp, as it refuses every key that makes a document an entry point.

The wire is one document holding several messages, because they share a vocabulary and a $ref may not leave a document here. A group therefore names the document and the member inside it that its fixtures pin, so a fixture still pins one message rather than something the wire allows somewhere.

A valid fixture is taken from the documentation's own printed message wherever the documentation prints one. The wire's first version was built from its own examples instead and refused the page's task message in four places, which is the failure this fixture exists to make impossible.

valid.covers: apiVersion, kind, metadata, steps.image, steps.outputs
the whole entry point
script, before_script, after_script, shell, files
files: a directory, ** and * in a glob, a glob relocated into a directory with a mode, a file relocated to a path of its own
mcp block
retain grammar
include, hidden blocks, extends
merge, strategy, and the per-step execution settings
workflow step keyword, concurrency, triggers
timeout at the root, which bounds the whole run, beside the step limit of the same name
a step name of 255 characters, a sub-workflow called with each half of its reference at 255, and a port, the edge naming it and a workflow output of 250, each the longest it may be

on.schedule with a stepped, a ranged and a named field, a timezone and its absence, jitter and catch_up; on.webhook with hmac, several segments, a sync response naming a declared output, and map; on.event with type, source and filter, and with another namespace's events filling an input by map; concurrency cancelling the run in progress

invalid.rule: A key at the root of the file that the language does not define.
A language version the reader does not know. apiVersion is read before anything else, so a file cannot ask to be read by rules that do not exist.
A workflow entry point declaring another kind. The same apiVersion covers the brick manifest, so the kind is what tells a reader which of the two it holds.
A workflow with no name. The name and the namespace form the identity a run, a grant and a git remote are addressed by.

A namespace named after a word the API routes on. The API's first path segment decides the route, so auth, me, users, groups, service-accounts, namespaces, runners, runner-pools, bus, tasks, bricks, runs, artifacts and stats cannot name a namespace.
A step name that is not an identifier. The name is used in needs, in expressions and in the run detail, so it stays to letters, digits, hyphens and underscores.
A step name of 256 characters. A step becomes a directory of its task's work directory, and no filesystem holds a name longer than 255.
An output port of 251 characters. A port becomes the file <name>.json, which a filesystem holds to 255 characters with its suffix.
A sub-workflow called by a name of 256 characters. Each half of <namespace>/<name> is a name, at most 255 characters, and a maxLength would bound the whole reference, so the pattern counts each half.
A workflow included from a namespace of 256 characters. Each half of <namespace>/<name> is a name, at most 255 characters.
A workflow output of 251 characters. A workflow output becomes the file <name>.json, as a port does, which a filesystem holds to 255 characters with its suffix.
A step keyword the language does not define. The set of step keywords is closed, so a misspelling is refused rather than silently ignored.
A step that both runs an image and calls a sub-workflow. workflow is an alternative to image, never a companion to it.
A step that calls a sub-workflow and also carries a script. script commands run inside image and workflow is an alternative to image, so a sub-workflow call has no container for a script to run in.

A step parameter name that is not an identifier. A parameter name is a key of /agk/params.json and is exported as AGK_PARAM_<NAME> when the step runs a script, so it cannot carry a hyphen. The brick manifest keys its own params by the same grammar, and a script step has no manifest to be validated against, so this document is the only one that catches the name.

A CPU request written as a number. It is written as a string so that half a core reads as 0.5 wherever it travels, in the workflow file, in the brick manifest and in the task message alike; brick/invalid/resources-cpu-not-a-string.yaml pins the same refusal on the other document.
An extends naming a block whose name does not start with a dot. Only a hidden block can be extended, and a hidden block is exactly a name that starts with a dot and is never executed.
An upstream state that is not one of succeeded, failed, skipped or always.
A retryable failure kind outside transient, failed, lost and timeout.
A key join that does not say what it matches items on. Without it, unmatched items cannot be told from matched ones.
A batch fan-out that does not say how many items go into a batch. The size is written in the parentheses, as batch(50).
A batch fan-out of no items. batch(n) is one container per batch of n items, and a batch of zero describes a shard that can never be filled.
A fetch count on something that is not a workflow output. Only a workflow output can be one-shot: an artifact travelling between two steps is read once per shard and again by a replay.

A one-shot output saying how many fetches it survives and not how long it lives. The two mechanisms compose: a one-shot artifact still has a duration, which is what expires it when nobody ever comes for it.
A fetch count of zero, which would declare an output that may never be collected. A one-shot output is fetches: 1, and two consumers are fetches: 2.
A duration written as a bare number. A duration carries its unit, so that a file says 10m where a reader would otherwise have to work out what 600 means.
A run timeout written in weeks. A duration is a number and one of the five units the language carries, ms, s, m, h or d, so a fortnight is written 14d.
A workflow output naming a step but not the port it is taken from. An output is a view of one step port, because an output that concatenated several would hide which step produced what.
A workflow include with no ref. A moving ref would let another repository change what this workflow does without this commit changing.
An include that is both a file of this repository and another repository. A path include resolves inside the same commit and a workflow include resolves elsewhere at a ref; one entry cannot be both.
A path include pinned to a ref. A path include resolves inside the same commit, so it can never be stale and there is nothing for a ref to pin.
A timeout on an async tool, where it would mean nothing: the call returns the run identifier at once.
A tool input taken from a step port. A tool is a view of the workflow's own boundary, never of the graph, which is what keeps the graph free to change beneath a published tool.
A published tool with no description. The description is the field a model acts on, so a tool without one is published to nobody's benefit.
A network posture outside none, egress and internal. Every task gets its own network, and there is no posture that puts a container on the host's.
An egress entry naming a host and no port. The runner proxy enforces the list as host and port pairs.
An egress entry whose port is outside 1 to 65535. The runner proxy opens a connection to the pair, and there is no port above that to open.
A runner selector that is not a label. Selectors are written as key=value, because that is what a runner's labels are.
A memory ceiling with no unit. Memory is a quantity with a binary suffix, so that 512Mi cannot be read as 512 bytes.

A secret written with the store it is read from. The namespace declares where each of its secrets lives, provider and path, and is confined to its own paths; the file names a secret and nothing more, so that pushing a workflow cannot aim it at whatever the store holds.

A secret named by where it sits in the store. A secret is named on the identifier grammar, the name a step mounts it by and the namespace declares it under, and where its value lives belongs to that declaration rather than to the file.
A cron expression that is not five fields. A schedule is a five-field expression read in the timezone given beside it.
A webhook authenticating by a means the engine does not offer. auth is hmac, bearer, mtls or none, and it proves which caller is speaking, never which user.
A cycle in the graph. Cycles are rejected at validation, before registration; looping is done by calling a sub-workflow.
An edge coming from a step the workflow does not declare. An edge is the only form of dependency there is, so it has to name something that exists.
An edge taking an output port nobody declares. normalize publishes ok and rejected, and an edge cannot invent a third port on it.
A step declaring an output port its brick manifest does not carry. outputs must be a subset of the ports the manifest declares.
A step feeding an input port nobody declares. The runner mounts one directory per port the brick declares, and there is no directory for a port the manifest never named.
A workflow output taken from a step the workflow does not declare.
A step mounting a secret the workflow never names. Secrets are mounted by the name the secrets block lists them under, and only secrets the owning namespace declares can be named there.
A script step that declares no output port. The image is a base image, no manifest is read and nothing about its ports is inferred, so outputs must be declared.
A tool input naming something the workflow does not declare.
A tool whose input is a workflow input carrying no schema. A tool has to publish an inputSchema, so the input it maps has to have one.
Two published tools carrying the same name. A tool identifier is unique within the workflow, because clients hold it.

A sync tool waiting longer than the ceiling. A sync call is capped at 120 seconds because clients time out, and a workflow that cannot finish inside it has to be async. The value is a literal in this file, so the ceiling is carried by the grammar of the timeout rather than left to the validator.
An expression reading a context root that is not exposed. The roots are workflow, run, trigger, event, vars, inputs, steps, item, matrix and secrets.
An expression reading item where the step is not sharded per item. item is available only under fan_out: item, which is what keeps the controller from loading a namespace's data in order to schedule.
A condition reading a secret. secrets is exposed to params and to secrets and nowhere else, and a secret is never reachable from a condition.

A file relocated to a relative path. Inside a container there is no directory a relative path could be relative to, the runner refuses one, and the task message holds that field to the same absolute grammar.
A cron field written in a syntax no five-field cron reads. ? and L belong to other schedulers' grammars, and a schedule is read the same way by everyone who reads it.
A cron value stepped on its own. Some crons read 5/15 as 5-59/15 and others refuse it, so a step follows * or a range and the file says which.
A cron field naming a minute past the hour's last. Each field is bounded by what it counts, and a value outside it names an occurrence that never comes.
A schedule read in the installation's own zone. One file would fire at different instants on two installations, so a schedule names its zone or is read in UTC.
A schedule's zone written as an offset. An offset does not move with daylight saving, which is what a named zone is for.
A schedule's zone the time zone database does not hold. The name is well formed and names no zone, so no instant can be read from it.
A sync webhook naming no output. A sync response returns one workflow output, and the trigger says which.
A webhook naming an output it never returns. An async response answers with the run id before any output exists.
A sync webhook returning an output the workflow does not declare. What a caller is answered with is one of the workflow's own outputs.
A webhook filling an input the workflow does not declare. map builds the run's inputs, each validated against its schema before the run exists, and an input nobody declared has none.
A webhook path with a .. segment. Normalised by a proxy on its way in, it would climb out of the namespace's prefix.
Two webhooks answering one path with one method. A request would start whichever the engine found first, so a path and a method answer one trigger.
An event trigger naming nothing it listens for. It would start a run on every event its namespace can see, so a subscription names a type, a source or a filter.
An event trigger naming only the namespace it listens to. It would start a run on every event published there, so a subscription names a type, a source or a filter whichever namespace it hears.
An event trigger filling an input the workflow does not declare. map builds the run's inputs, each validated against its schema before the run exists, and an input nobody declared has none.
A concurrency policy whose cancel_in_progress is not a boolean. The arriving run either waits or cancels, and there is no third answer.

valid.covers: hidden blocks at the root of an included file, a matrix in a block
include, vars, secrets, defaults, steps with a hidden block and a step among them, a hidden block at the root; the root agentiik.yaml of a library repository a workflow include reads

invalid.rule: apiVersion in an included file. An included file is a fragment, not an entry point: it has no apiVersion, no kind and no metadata.
kind in an included file. An included file is a fragment, not an entry point: it has no apiVersion, no kind and no metadata.
metadata in an included file. An included file is a fragment, not an entry point: the name and the namespace are the including workflow's, and a fragment has no metadata.
inputs in an included file. What a workflow is given is its boundary, declared by the workflow itself, so that reading one file tells you what that workflow is.
outputs in an included file. What a workflow returns is its boundary, declared by the workflow itself, so that reading one file tells you what that workflow is.
on in an included file. What starts a workflow is its boundary, declared by the workflow itself, so that reading one file tells you what that workflow is.

An mcp block in an included file. Reuse applies to steps and defaults; the published surface is declared by the workflow that publishes it, so that reading one file tells you everything that workflow exposes. This fixture is the included file itself, named by an entry point as include: [{ path: ./common-bricks.yaml }].
concurrency in an included file. How runs of a workflow queue behind one another is the workflow's own, declared where the workflow is, so that reading one file tells you what that workflow is.
timeout at the root of an included file. The bound on a whole run is the workflow's own, declared where the workflow is; a step's timeout belongs in defaults or on the step.
A key an included file does not define. An included file is closed like every block the language owns, so a misspelling is refused rather than quietly doing nothing.

valid.covers: the worked manifest of the brick contract, embedded in an image at /agk/brick.yaml
the manifest the workflow fixtures on ports are checked against: two input ports, two output ports, a port declared without a schema
the smallest manifest the contract accepts: an identity and the account the container runs as

a secret mounted under a file name carrying a dot, as a key file naturally does, and a secret whose mount is not its name: the mount the task message and the grant redemption then carry on the same grammar
a port declared with a name of 250 characters, the longest a port may be, since it becomes the file <name>.json

invalid.rule: A manifest declaring another kind. A brick manifest and a workflow entry point are both YAML carrying an apiVersion, and the kind is what tells one from the other before anything else is read.
A brick version that is not a semantic version. The version moves with the brick and not with the image tag, and it is what a person reads to know which release a digest holds.
A brick name that is not lowercase and hyphenated. The name is what a person types and what the catalog page is filed under.
A manifest that says nothing about what it needs from its container. The runner builds the host configuration from the runtime block.
A key under spec that the contract does not define.
A runtime block that does not say which account the container runs as. It is required because the rule that refuses root has to have something to read.
A manifest declaring root. It is refused here and checked again at publication, because a read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities are worth little to a process running as uid 0.
The same refusal written as a uid and a gid: uid 0 is root whatever it is spelled as.
A network posture outside none, egress and internal.
A port name of 251 characters. A port becomes the file <name>.json under /agk/out/ports/, which a filesystem holds to 255 characters with its suffix, and a workflow could not name it.
A port name carrying a comma. A port name becomes a directory under /agk/in/, a file name under /agk/out/ports/ and one entry of the comma separated AGK_OUT_PORTS.
A port carrying a key other than its schema. What a step must feed is decided by the workflow, not asserted by the port.
A parameter name that is not an identifier. A parameter name is a key of /agk/params.json and is exported as AGK_PARAM_<NAME> when a step runs a script, so it cannot carry a hyphen.
A secret mounted somewhere other than /agk/secrets/<name>. The runner mounts secret values on tmpfs there, and nowhere else.

A secret mounted at /agk/secrets/.., which names the parent of the secrets directory rather than a file in it. A mount's file name begins with a letter or a digit, so a dot inside a name is kept and a name made of dots is refused.
A CPU request written as a number. It is written as a string so that half a core reads as 0.5 wherever it travels, in the manifest and in the task message alike.

valid.covers: the worked envelope of the data exchange model, with the digest the documentation elides written out in full
the envelope a declared port publishes when the container never writes it, and the one every port of a skipped step publishes
a batch published by a second attempt, carrying one item with no payload of its own and nothing attached
a batch from a step whose name is 255 characters, the longest a name the workflow file writes may be

invalid.rule: An envelope with no metadata. A task is self-contained and a runner never sees the graph it came from, so the run, the step and the port travel with the data instead of being looked up.
An envelope whose items are not a list. Order is part of the contract: wait_all concatenates in edge declaration order and zip pairs by rank.
An item with no identifier. The identifier is what a shard, a replay and a run inspector speak about the same element by, once the batch has been split, concatenated or reordered.
An item with no files list. An item with nothing attached carries an empty list, so that a consumer never has to tell absent from empty.
An item whose data is not an object. The shape belongs to the port, declared by the schema the brick manifest gives it, and the envelope says only that it is an object.
An attempt numbered zero. Attempts count from 1, which is what separates the batch that was kept from the ones that failed before it.
A negative item count. The count is what a condition weighs a batch by without its contents ever being loaded.
Metadata carrying a key the envelope does not define. The shard index reaches a container as AGK_SHARD and does not travel in the envelope.

An envelope naming a step of 256 characters. A step becomes a directory, and no filesystem holds a name longer than 255; workflow/invalid/step-name-256-characters.yaml refuses the name where it is written and this refuses it where it travels.

An envelope naming a port that carries a comma. The name becomes a directory under /agk/in/, a file name under /agk/out/ports/ and one entry of the comma separated AGK_OUT_PORTS; brick/invalid/port-name-with-comma.yaml refuses the declaration and this refuses the same name on the wire.

An attached file whose digest is the documentation's typographic elision rather than a digest. The digest is the artifact's address, so it is sixty-four lowercase hexadecimal characters and never an abbreviation of one.
An attached file with no digest. The digest is also the artifact's address: it is what the physical key sha256/<digest> is built from, and what a consumer checks its transfer against.

valid.covers: the whole message: the run and the step, the image resolved to a digest, the parameters with the secret material taken out, the secrets by name and mount point, the inputs by digest, the ports, the ceilings, the posture, the labels, the deadline and the grant
shard, the five-segment idempotency key it produces, and egress_allow beside network: egress

the message the documentation prints, identifiers and all: it elides them to fifteen and twelve characters, and a schema that imposed the twenty-six a ULID is minted at would refuse the page it was written from
script, before_script, after_script, shell, files, timeout, idempotent and cache_key: what a runner needs for a step whose image is a base image rather than a brick

the files of the load step the documentation prints: the short form of a selector, a path or glob with no to because the step asked for no relocation and the file stays where it is under /agk/repo/, beside a long form that relocates one
a secret whose mount carries a dot, client.key, on the grammar the brick manifest declared it on and the grant redemption answers it on

invalid.rule: a secret entry is a name and a mount point and never a value: the message names what a step mounts and carries none of it, and the entry is closed so that a value has no key to be written under
an input is named by port, digest and count; the URLs come from redeeming the grant, so a copy of the message is worth nothing on its own
a tag is resolved once for the whole run, so what reaches a runner is a digest: two tasks of one run cannot end up on two builds because a tag moved between them
an attempt is counted from one, so an idempotency key naming attempt zero names no attempt
the grant is what turns the names in the message into values, and a message without one asks a runner to do work it cannot fetch the inputs for
a namespace is never one of the words the API's first path segment routes on, so a message naming runs as its namespace names one no run can be owned by

a mount is one file directly under /agk/secrets/, and .. names the parent of that directory rather than a file in it: a file name begins with a letter or a digit, so a dot inside it is kept and a name made of dots is refused

valid.covers: a task that ran and failed, as the page prints it: the state, the exit code, the instants, the empty lists of ports and artifacts a failed task reports, the log and the usage
a task declared lost, which carries no exit code and no result of its own, because it is the absence of three heartbeats that declares it

a task stopped at its deadline, which carries the exit code its stop left, 137 after the grace ran out, since its container started and exited: the ending the wire could not express until the page named all nine states
a success whose container exited before the first sample of its statistics was read, which reports the image pull and neither sampled figure rather than zeros nobody measured

invalid.rule: a result is terminal: running is a state a task passes through and never one it ends in, and the heartbeat is what says a task is still running
queued is a run state, not a task state, and the two vocabularies are separate on purpose
cpu_seconds and max_rss_bytes are read off the same samples, so a usage block carries both or neither

valid.covers: a runner saying the container of a task it holds has started
a runner saying the container has exited and its outputs are being collected and uploaded

invalid.rule: progress is running or publishing and never an ending, which only a result reports
progress never carries state, the keyword a result is told apart by, so that no document is both a result and a progress message

valid.covers: the join exchange: the token, the public key, the labels claimed, the capacity and the architecture, answered with a runner identifier and a long-lived credential

invalid.rule: the runner generates a keypair locally and sends the public key; the private key never leaves the machine, so the request is closed against one

valid.covers: the ten second heartbeat: the idempotency keys the host holds, answered with what it is to stop and whether it is draining

invalid.rule: a heartbeat lists idempotency keys, and a key without its attempt names no attempt at anything

valid.covers: a rotation as the agent makes it: the runner and the time signed by its key, answered with a new credential and its rotate_by

invalid.rule: the credential a rotation renews is the bearer credential of the call and never a field of the request, which is closed

valid.covers: redeeming one task's grant: the input URLs, the secret values, the upload URLs and the repository tree the step will see
a secret value answered for a mount carrying a dot, client.key, which the task message and the brick manifest already accepted and this answer used to refuse

invalid.rule: a file mode is octal, written the way the workflow file writes it, because the wire echoes a value that file wrote

a secret value is written at its mount, and a mount of .. would write it over the parent of /agk/secrets/ rather than into a file under it: the grammar that keeps a dot inside a name still refuses a name made of dots

valid.covers: one chunk of a running task's captured standard error, with what makes two chunks orderable and a redelivered one harmless

invalid.rule: the credential and the grant authenticate the call and are members of neither half: a token written into a body is a token that ends up in the very log this message carries

valid.covers: a pool and the token issued from it: the labels, the namespaces it accepts, the ceilings, the single use and the expiry

invalid.rule: a label is key=value, and a runner may only ever claim labels its token allowed, so a half written one is refused before it can be claimed

valid.covers: a stop as the controller publishes it on agentiik.stops: the key of the task in flight and one of the four reasons

invalid.rule: a reason is why a task is stopped and not what it ends as: timed_out is the state a deadline stop ends in, and deadline is the reason

valid.covers: a user: a login, a display name, and whether the account is an administrator's or suspended
a user who has signed in, with when they last did, as GET /api/v1/users/{login} answers it
a group of users, by login, as the documentation's team-finance is
the built-in identity of a namespace, NS/agentiik, which scheduled, webhook and event runs are attributed to and which nobody created
a user the policy suspended for holding no passkey when passwords came to be forbidden, which an enrolment link or a recovery code lifts, as GET /api/v1/users/{login} answers it
a login of 255 characters, the most a namespace's name holds, since a login is also the name of its personal namespace

a user who said who they are and set a photo: given and family names, a title, a location, an IANA time zone, a bio, and when the photo was last set, as GET /api/v1/me answers it once PATCH /api/v1/me and PUT /api/v1/me/avatar wrote them
a user an administrator gave an email address, at POST /api/v1/users or PATCH /api/v1/users/{login}, shown by the display name their given and family names make

invalid.rule: operator is refused as a login: it is the principal the v0.2.5 operator token wrote on the rows it touched, and those rows keep it
installation is refused as a login: it names the installation itself as the author of the pool default, and a user of that name would read as that author
a login is also the name of its personal namespace, so the words the API's first path segment routes on cannot be one
a user record never carries what the user proves themselves with; the object is closed so that a hash cannot be written into it
a display name is one line holding no control character, since it is printed at a terminal, where a line break forges a line of its own
a group is a named set of users, so its members are logins and a group reference is not one
suspended_for says why an account is suspended, so an account that is not suspended carries none
stats is reserved from v0.3.0, for GET /api/v1/stats/pools which v0.6.0 serves, and a login is also the name of its personal namespace
a login is at most 255 characters, the most a directory or a bus subject token holds a name to, since it is also the name of its personal namespace
a bio is one line holding no control character, since it is printed at a terminal beside the name, where a line break forges a line of its own
a title is at most 128 characters, a line on a card beside the name
an email address is one @ with something on each side, and one holding two is not an address
an email address holds no space or control character, since no address does and it is printed at a terminal
an email address is at most 254 characters, the longest a mail path carries once its two angle brackets are counted

valid.covers: a user, named by login
a group, named group:NAME
a service account, named NS/NAME, here the namespace's built-in identity
a group whose name is 255 characters, the most a name holds
a service account whose namespace and name are each 255 characters, the most a name holds

invalid.rule: operator names the v0.2.5 operator token on the rows it wrote and is no principal a grant or a token can name
installation names the installation itself as the author of the pool default, and is no principal a grant or a token can name
a user is named by the bare login; only a group carries a prefix, and a login holds no colon
a group's name is written on the namespace grammar, lowercase words joined by hyphens
a group's name is at most 255 characters, as a namespace's is, inside its reference as anywhere
each half of a service account reference is at most 255 characters, as a namespace's name is

valid.covers: a device-bound passkey: Backup Eligibility clear, so the kind is device-bound
a synced passkey: Backup Eligibility set, so the kind is synced, with its last use
a password, described by its existence and never by its hash
a TOTP generator, described by its existence and never by its shared secret

invalid.rule: the kind is recorded from the Backup Eligibility flag, and a credential eligible for backup is a synced passkey whatever it is called
Backup State can only be set where Backup Eligibility is, as Web Authentication defines the two flags the kind is recorded from
a credential is described and never held: the hash stays in the database, and forbidding passwords deletes it

valid.covers: a user's token as it is listed: its expiry 90 days out, its last use and its device label, and no value
a service account's token narrowed to two permissions on one workflow, expiring a year out, the longest allowed

invalid.rule: a token is stored hashed and shown once, so the record a listing returns cannot carry its value
an API token is a bearer credential with an expiry, and one that never ends is one nobody remembers to revoke
a scope narrows the principal's rights, and an empty one narrows nothing while reading as if it did: absent is how a token says it keeps them all
a token lasts at most a year from its creation, a rule between two values of one record that JSON Schema cannot hold, so the API holds it
a token is held by a user or a service account, never a group, which holds no credential of its own: a group's token would be a way in that belongs to nobody

valid.covers: the documentation's Terraform grant: team-ops runs monthly-invoicing as operator until an expiry
a namespace-scope grant, inherited by every workflow inside, written by the bootstrap token before any administrator existed
the documentation's deny: alice, an editor of finance through team-finance, loses run:read_data on monthly-invoicing and keeps the rest of the role there, whatever any allow gives
the owner grant a user's personal namespace is created with at their first sign-in, written by the installation, since nobody asked for it

invalid.rule: a grant binds one role or denies one permission, never both, so that revoking one row never revokes half of another
a deny names a permission, as the documentation's deny of run:read_data does, and not a role
the roles are viewer, operator, editor and owner; being an administrator is a property of a user and never a role on a scope
a scope is a namespace or one workflow in it, and a reserved word can never name a namespace
the namespace half of a workflow's scope is a namespace's name, at most 255 characters

valid.covers: the run role, which deliberately lacks workflow:read
the role that can share, holding grant:manage

invalid.rule: four roles and no more; an administrator is a user property with no implicit run:read_data

valid.covers: the permission a deny most often names, written with its underscore
the permission that makes owner the role that can share

invalid.rule: identifiers are never prettified: the permission is run:read_data in the YAML, the API, the HCL and the prose
a permission is one of nine atoms; a wildcard would grant whatever atom is added next, which deny by default forbids

valid.covers: the documentation's finance namespace with all six quotas, owned by a group
a personal namespace, named after its owner's login, with the two quotas every namespace holds at their defaults
a namespace from before v0.3.0, shared and owned by nobody, since v0.2 had nobody to name, with the two quotas it held then
a namespace requiring device-bound passkeys, and one more of them, of everyone holding a grant in it
a namespace renamed twice, listing the names it left in the order it left them, the first a word reserved since it was created before v0.3.0, which a former name may be, and a picture set

invalid.rule: the API's first path segment decides the route, so a reserved word cannot name a namespace
a personal namespace belongs to one user, named after their login
a personal namespace is its user's, so it always names its owner; only a shared namespace from before v0.3.0 names none
a personal namespace is named after its owner's login, a rule between two values of one record that the API holds
a quota bounds what a namespace consumes and starts at one; stopping a namespace is what removing its grants or its pools is for
absent allows every pool that accepts the namespace, and a pool's own empty list of namespaces means every one, so an empty list here is refused rather than read
the quotas are the six the documentation lists; a seventh would be a bound the engine never enforces

a namespace may tighten the installation's policy and never loosen it, so allowing passwords where the installation forbids them is refused; it needs the installation's policy beside this record, so the API holds it
a namespace's name is at most 255 characters, the most a directory or a bus subject token holds a name to
a namespace holds each name it left once, and lists it once
a rename back to a former name takes it out of the list, since it is the namespace's name again, a rule between two values of one record that the API holds

valid.covers: the installation defaults, written out: password as a fallback, a passkey required, user verification required, synced passkeys accepted, two passkeys before a password may go
passwords turned off and synced passkeys refused, every other key at its default
a policy that states nothing, which is every default

invalid.rule: min_passkeys is what a user must hold before the password may go, and zero would let it go from an account with nothing to replace it
no TOTP on top of a passkey: with user verification required an assertion already proves two factors, so the policy has no TOTP setting
user_verification is required or preferred; Web Authentication's discouraged would make a passkey one factor

valid.covers: an administrator having granted themselves editor in finance for a day, told to the namespace's owner with the grant they wrote, the act, granted, and who did it

an administrator having put dave in a group holding viewer in finance, told to the namespace's owner with the group's grant, written by somebody else long before, joined_group, who did it and the user put in

the bootstrap token having put dave in a group holding editor in finance, told as by operator, the one act of the token's that is told, since a grant it writes is told to nobody, the token owning every namespace
a sign-in refused because a passkey's signature counter did not move forward, told to its user with the passkey's credential ID and no namespace
agentiik-api recover having issued the administrator alice a recovery code from the installation's host, told to every administrator with her login and nothing else

invalid.rule: a sign-in names no namespace, so a refused sign-in's notification carries none; each kind carries what its reader needs and nothing of the other's
an owner told of an administrator widening their own access is told which grant they wrote, so that it can be read and revoked
an owner told of an administrator widening access is told which act did it, since the grant alone does not say: a group's grant was written long before, and a deny lifted names whoever wrote it
an owner told of an administrator widening access is told who did it, which the grant's granted_by need not be
a user put in a group is named to the owners told of it, who could not learn otherwise who now holds the group's role, since the group routes are an administrator's alone
login names the user put in a group, on joined_group alone; any other act names nobody put anywhere
a sign-in refused for a passkey's counter was no administrator's act, so it names none and nobody who did it; each kind carries what its reader needs and nothing of the other's
every administrator is told which account the break-glass path issued a recovery code, since an administrator who did not run it has to know whose it was

valid.covers: a repository created from v0.4.0: protected, its default branch pushed to, labels read from its entry point
a workflow from before v0.4.0: unprotected, its default branch unborn until a git push fills it

invalid.rule: A head written as an abbreviation. A commit is written whole, since an abbreviation is a name another commit can come to share.
A default branch git would refuse as a ref name.
A repository that does not say whether its default branch is protected, which decides who may move it.

valid.covers: a protected default branch and who last moved it
a tag, peeled to its commit, moved by a service account
the unborn default branch of a repository nothing was pushed to

invalid.rule: An unborn branch naming who moved it. Nobody has moved a branch that points at no commit.
A ref named without refs/heads/ or refs/tags/, which leaves a branch and a tag of one name indistinguishable.
A remote-tracking ref. A workflow repository holds branches and tags alone.

valid.covers: a commit a git push carried, with its parent and its pusher
a version agk push sent as a tree before v0.4.0, by the bootstrap token, with no parent named
a library's commit, which other workflows include and nothing runs

invalid.rule: A version arriving by neither git nor a tree push.
A version saying it is no library. The flag is written where a commit is a library's and left out otherwise, so that one shape is not two.
A version naming nobody who pushed it. The pusher answers for what it names, secrets included.

valid.covers: a run a schedule started, attributed to its namespace's built-in identity, finished
a run a person asked for, still queued, with neither a start nor an end
a run another workflow called, naming the calling run and step, and attributed to the principal its caller is

invalid.rule: A run another workflow called that names no caller. A call is a run asking, and its callee's reader is owed which one.
A run a person asked for naming a calling run. Only a call from another workflow has a caller, so from is one shape for one kind.
A run started by a kind the Triggers table does not name. cron is a field of a schedule, and the kind is schedule.
A run attributed to no principal. Every run is let in by the grants of the principal it is attributed to, so one naming nobody is one nobody can account for.
A run carrying its trigger kind as trigger. An expression reads run.trigger_kind, and an identifier is the same string in the YAML, the API and the schema.

valid.covers: the documentation's local run as its version resolves it: a path and a workflow include, a fan-out, two edges on one port, a script step, an extended block, outputs with retention, a schedule

invalid.rule: An image by tag. A version names every image by the digest its tag was resolved to at the push, so that a tag moved since changes nothing a run runs.
A step running an image and calling a sub-workflow. A step carries an image or a call and never both.
A brick step naming no brick. A brick step is held to its manifest at the push, and the graph says which release that was.
A workflow include without the commit its ref resolved to. A run records it, so that another repository moving a tag changes nothing the version does.
A file relocated to a relative path, which the runner refuses.
A brick step carrying before_script and shell. A brick runs its own entry point, so the script keywords a defaults block writes reach a script step alone.

repositories.description: The repository kind. Each case is one push of a workflow repository, judged as the pre-receive hook judges the commit at a pushed tip, and it pins either the graph that commit resolves to or the one refusal it meets. A case is a directory rather than a document, because what it pins is about several documents together: the entry point and the files it includes, the repositories a workflow include reads, and what the hook reads from the installation, which the case holds as stand-ins. A case under valid/ carries expected.json and one under invalid/ refusal.json, never both. agk validate and agk push make the same checks where they reach the stores the hook reads, and a case says nothing of what they do where they do not. An invalid case says what else refuses the file its refusal is about, as the other groups say it of a document: schema where the file's own schema, the workflow's or the fragment's, refuses it too, and validator where only the hook can, a rule about the graph, the tree or the installation; every other YAML file of a case is one its schema accepts.

layout.tree/: The files of the pushed commit's tree, as they would be committed, each with mode 100644: the entry point at tree/agentiik.yaml where the case has one, the files it includes, and whatever else the commit carries. A YAML file there is an entry point where it is named agentiik.yaml or agentiik.yml, and a fragment otherwise. No name in a case begins with a dot or an underscore, which go:embed leaves out of an embedded tree.
layout.tree.json: Present where the tree holds entries that cannot be files here, listed as formats.tree describes them. The tree pushed is tree/ with them added.
layout.case.json: The repository and the commit pushed, and the stand-ins for the installation: the repository's pins and brick manifests, the namespace's secret declarations, the versions already recorded and the other repositories an include reads, as formats.case describes them.
layout.manifests/: The brick manifests the repository's store holds, each a document valid against brick.schema.json and named by case.json's manifests.
layout.repositories/: The trees of the other repositories a workflow include reads, one directory per commit, named by case.json's repositories.
layout.expected.json: A valid case's resolved graph, valid against wire.schema.json#/$defs/resolvedGraph: what the hook records for the pushed commit, and what the API answers for it.
layout.refusal.json: An invalid case's refusal, as formats.refusal describes it.

case.title: Case
case.description: What the hook is told beside the pushed tree: which repository and which commit the push is for, and what it reads from the installation. Each of the last is a stand-in for a store the installation keeps, the pins and manifests per repository and the secret declarations per namespace, holding exactly what the case needs and nothing a real store would add, so that a consumer builds the store from it and nothing else.

namespace.description: The namespace the repository belongs to: what metadata.namespace has to equal where the file writes it, and whose secret declarations the hook reads.

repository.description: The name of the repository pushed to, which metadata.name has to equal: the name is the identity runs, grants and the git remote are addressed by, and the repository already holds one. It is also the repository whose pins and manifests the hook reads.

commit.description: The commit at the pushed tip, whole, whose tree is tree/ with the entries of tree.json: the commit expected.json records. It is a label rather than the hash git computes from the tree, so a consumer pushing the tree with git maps the commit it gets onto this one, and so for the commits of other repositories.

versions.description: Commits of this repository already recorded as versions. A push of one of them is answered as the version it is, whatever its tree holds, an entry point below the root among them, and is not judged again by a rule added after it was stored. The version is rebuilt from tree/ and the stand-ins of this case, so a stored case names every image by digest and needs neither a pin nor a manifest from them. Absent where the repository holds none.

pins.description: The repository's image pins: each reference a step may name an image by that is not a digest, mapped to the reference by digest it was pinned to, of that reference's own repository. The hook reaches no registry, so a step naming a reference no pin holds is refused, and a step naming a digest needs none.

manifests.description: The repository's brick manifests: each image by digest mapped to the file under manifests/ holding the manifest recorded for it, valid against brick.schema.json. A brick step is held to the manifest of its image once pinned; a script step reads none.

secrets.description: The names of the secrets the namespace declares, without where they live, which the hook does not read. Every secret the workflow names has to be among them.

repositories.description: The other repositories a workflow include reads, by <namespace>/<name>, each with its refs and the tree at every commit they name. Absent where the tree includes none.

refs.description: The repository's branches and tags, each written in full and mapped to the commit it points at, a tag peeled to its commit. An include's ref is read as a tag of that name, or as a commit a tree below is given for.

trees.description: The tree of each commit a ref names, as the directory under repositories/ holding its files, the root agentiik.yaml among them.

tree.title: Tree listing
tree.description: The entries of the pushed tree that cannot be files of tree/, each with the mode git records for it: an executable file, which tree/ does not hold so that every file there is 100644, and a symbolic link, a submodule and a name that is not UTF-8, which are what the hook refuses and none of which survives being committed here: git commits a link as a link, which a checkout without symbolic links writes as a plain file and go:embed refuses to embed; a submodule would make this repository depend on another; and a name that is not UTF-8 cannot be created on a filesystem that holds names to UTF-8, macOS's among them, nor carried by a Go module. The tree a case pushes is tree/ with these entries added, and no entry names a path tree/ already holds.

path.description: The entry's path from the root of the tree, as bytes: a printable ASCII character other than % as itself, and any other byte as % and two uppercase hexadecimal digits, never a byte that has a character of its own, / among them, and never a null byte, which no name holds. A JSON document carries UTF-8 text alone, and a name that is not UTF-8 is what the listing is for. scripts/caf%E9.py is café.py written in Latin-1.

mode.description: The mode git records for the entry: 100644 a file, 100755 an executable file, 120000 a symbolic link, 160000 a submodule.

target.description: What a symbolic link points to, the bytes git stores as its blob, written as path is. A link alone carries it.

commit.description: The commit a submodule records, whole. A submodule alone carries it.

content.description: A file's content, as UTF-8 text. A file alone carries it.

refusal.title: Refusal
refusal.description: What the hook refuses an invalid case by: one rule, and where. The hook writes it on git's error stream as file:line:column: message (rule), or as file: message (rule) where it names no place in the file, and the ref stays where it was. The message is the engine's to word and is not pinned here.

rule.description: The rule, spelled as graph.Rule values are: the name the fixture corpus files a fixture under, where it has one. The hook refuses by more rules than package graph names today, the tree's and the installation's among them.

oneOf.description: A path include naming a file outside the repository tree. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A path include naming a file the commit does not hold. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
An include coming back to a file that is still being resolved. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

An included file carrying apiVersion, which makes a document an entry point; spelled after the fragment group's fixture, as the engine's mcp-in-included-file is. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

An included file declaring inputs, which are the workflow's own boundary; spelled after the fragment group's fixture, as the engine's mcp-in-included-file is. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A cycle among the steps. The engine's package graph names it today.
An edge, or a workflow output, taking a port its step does not publish. The engine's package graph names it today.
A brick step declaring an output port its manifest does not carry. The engine's package graph names it today.
A brick step whose image has no manifest the hook can read: for the hook, none recorded in the repository's store under the image's digest. The engine's package graph names it today.

A port past 250 characters, in the entry point, a file it includes or a brick manifest: a port a step publishes or is fed on, either end of an edge, the port a workflow output is taken from, a published tool's output; spelled after the workflow group's fixture that pins the same bound. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

A workflow output past 250 characters; spelled after the workflow group's fixture that pins the same bound. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

A secret the workflow names, in its secrets block or an included file's, that its namespace does not declare. The engine's secret-not-declared is another rule: a step mounting a secret the secrets block does not name. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A metadata.name other than the name of the repository pushed to. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A metadata.namespace, where the file writes one, other than the namespace the repository belongs to. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A tree holding no agentiik.yaml, at its root or anywhere else. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

A tree holding no agentiik.yaml at its root and at least one below it; the refusal names the one whose path comes first in byte order. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A symbolic link in the tree. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A submodule in the tree. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A name in the tree that is not UTF-8. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.
A step naming an image by a tag the repository's store holds no pin for. Named here first: the engine refuses it by no rule yet, and its hook is to refuse it by this one.

file.description: The path from the root of the tree of the file the refusal is about, or of the entry of the tree it is about, written as tree.json writes a path, which the hook writes as the bytes it stands for; for a tree without an entry point, agentiik.yaml, the file that is not there, and for one whose entry point is below the root, the file found there.

line.description: The line the refused node begins on, counted from 1, as a YAML 1.2 parser counts it: the value where the value is refused, a path an include names, a port, a name or an image; the key where writing the key at all is refused, apiVersion in an included file; and the key where the name refused is a key, a workflow output's. Absent where the refusal is about the file as a whole, an entry of the tree or something no one place in the file holds, a cycle.

column.description: The column that node begins at on its line, counted from 1 in characters. Written with line and only with it.

notes: Permissions are not part of a case. The pusher holds whatever the push needs, workflow:write, secret:use on every secret the tree names and workflow:read on every repository a workflow include reads; which of them a push needs follows from the tree, and a refusal for one missing is the API's to pin.

A case holds one fault, so that it pins one refusal: everything else in it is what a valid case holds, a pin for every image a step names by a tag, a manifest for every image a brick step runs, and a declaration for every secret the workflow names.

Rules are spelled as graph.Rule values are, the corpus's own name for the fixture pinning a rule where there is one. cycle-in-graph, edge-port-not-declared, step-output-not-in-manifest and manifest-missing are graph.Rule values today; the other names in formats.refusal are named here first, for the hook to refuse by, since it refuses by more rules than package graph names: the tree's, the installation's, the includes' and the bounds'.

The keys an included file may not carry are refused one rule each, as the fragment group files one fixture each and the engine already spells mcp-in-included-file: kind-in-included-file, metadata-in-included-file, outputs-in-included-file, on-in-included-file, concurrency-in-included-file and timeout-in-included-file, beside the two cases here. A rule joins formats.refusal with the first case that pins it.

The line and column of a refusal are checked to be where a node of the file begins, so that a position that no longer lands on a node after the file was edited fails the build rather than a consumer's test; one that lands on another node is the consumer's to catch.

A library repository, whose root agentiik.yaml is a fragment and whose tips are versions with no graph, has no case yet: expected.json is a resolved graph, and a push resolving to none needs a shape of its own, which the includes-across-repositories work settles.

valid.covers: includes applied in declaration order, each over the one before it and all of them under the entry point; what a file includes applied before the file itself; a file two others include applied once, where it is first reached, whether named beside the file naming it or from the root; a hidden block of one name replaced whole by a later file's; vars merged by name, defaults keyword by keyword; every file's secrets, each once, in the order first named

extends followed depth first, from a block in the entry point to one in an included file, and applied from the outermost block in; defaults above every block and below the step's own values; each keyword replaced whole by the next layer that writes it, resources and retry among them, and params merged by name

before_script and after_script merged outwards in: the defaults' commands first, then each block's from the outermost, then the step's own; the entry point's defaults.before_script replacing the included file's, as any keyword of defaults does; a brick step under the same defaults carrying none of the script keywords; shell as the step writes it

a step named with a leading dot is a hidden block: out of steps and order, never executed, and never held to the repository's pins and manifests; a chain of extends from a step through a hidden step to a hidden block at the root

a step written in an included file keeps its own values above defaults, its file's and the entry point's alike, and the entry point overrides it keyword by keyword, a keyword it does not write left as the included file wrote it; params merged by name across the two files

a workflow include read at the commit its tag resolves to, and not where a branch has moved since: the other repository's root agentiik.yaml read as a fragment, its own path includes resolved inside that repository at that commit, and the include recorded with the commit

a commit already recorded as a version, pushed again, answered as the version it is and not judged by the rules added after it was stored: a port of 251 characters, and a secret the namespace no longer declares

invalid.rule: A path include leaving the repository tree. A path include resolves inside the same commit, and nothing outside the tree is readable at all.

A path include naming a file the commit does not hold. A path include resolves against the directory of the file naming it, inside the same commit, so a file elsewhere in the tree is not the one it names.

An include coming back to a file that is still being resolved. A file cannot include itself, directly or through another, since its resolution would never end; the refusal names the include that closes the ring.
apiVersion in an included file. An included file is a fragment, not an entry point: it has no apiVersion, no kind and no metadata.
inputs in an included file. What a workflow is given is its boundary, declared by the workflow itself, so that reading one file tells you what that workflow is.
A cycle among the steps. Cycles are rejected at validation, before registration; looping is done by calling a sub-workflow.
An edge taking an output port its upstream step does not publish. An edge cannot invent a port on a step.
A brick step declaring an output port the manifest the repository's store holds for the image does not carry. outputs must be a subset of the ports the manifest declares.

A port of 251 characters, written in a file the entry point includes. A port becomes the file <name>.json, which a filesystem holds to 255 characters with its suffix, and the bound holds in the entry point, in every file it includes and in every brick manifest.
A workflow output of 251 characters. A workflow output becomes the file <name>.json, as a port does, which a filesystem holds to 255 characters with its suffix.

A secret the secrets block names that the namespace does not declare, refused although no step mounts it. A workflow can name only the secrets its own namespace declares, so that moving it elsewhere breaks the reference rather than carrying access along.
A metadata.name other than the name of the repository pushed to. The name is the identity runs, grants and the git remote are addressed by, and the repository already holds one.

A metadata.namespace other than the namespace the repository belongs to. A workflow reaches the secrets, the quotas and the runner pools of the namespace that owns it, and the file cannot move it to another.
A tree with no agentiik.yaml. The entry point is always at the root, and agentiik.yml is another file.

A tree whose only agentiik.yaml is below its root. The entry point is always at the root; a workflow kept in a directory of a larger repository is pushed as a repository of its own, which git subtree split --prefix billing makes.
A symbolic link in the tree. Its target would be resolved on whichever host lays the tree out, where it could point outside the repository.
A submodule in the tree. It is another repository, and a runner holds no credential to fetch it.
A name in the tree that is not UTF-8. A name travels as JSON text, where it would arrive as another name.

A step naming an image by a tag the repository's store holds no pin for, a pin of another tag of the same repository beside it. A server runs every image by the digest its tag was pinned to, and the hook reaches no registry to resolve one.
A brick step naming an image by a digest the repository's store holds no manifest for. A brick step is held to its manifest at the push, and reading one out of the image would be pulling it.
